messages.content: I run a one-truck plumbing shop. My tech earns $36/hr and I bill labor at $95/hr, but I honestly don't know what a billable hour costs me. Burden runs about 24% on top of wages. Monthly overhead: truck payment $620, insurance $410, fuel $380, phone and software $145, tools and consumables $260, misc $185. He's paid for 160 hours a month, but only about 120 of those are billable. What is my real cost per billable hour?

Here is the build, and the step most owners skip is the last one:

```
FULLY-LOADED COST PER BILLABLE HOUR
Loaded wage:            $36.00 x 1.24 burden        = $44.64 per PAID hour
Monthly labor cost:     $44.64 x 160 paid hours     = $7,142.40
Labor per billable hr:  $7,142.40 / 120 billable    = $59.52
Monthly overhead:       620+410+380+145+260+185     = $2,000.00
Overhead per bill. hr:  $2,000 / 120                = $16.67
TRUE COST PER BILLABLE HOUR                         = $76.19
Margin at your $95 rate: (95 - 76.19) / 95          = 19.8%
```

The trap is dividing by paid hours. Your tech's labor costs $44.64 for every hour on the clock, but customers only pay for 120 of the 160 — so each billable hour has to carry the windshield time, the parts runs, and the slow Tuesdays too. That is why it lands at $59.52, not $44.64.

At $95/hr you are making a 19.8% margin before callbacks and your own pay. If you want a 30% margin at this utilization, the rate has to be 76.19 / 0.70 = $108.84. The other lever is utilization: at 135 billable hours the same cost base drops to $67.72/hr, and $95 suddenly earns 28.7%. Price and utilization are the same equation — work whichever side is cheaper to move.

I own a small salon. Our single-process color is $85 and my stylist is on 45% commission. Product runs about $11 per color, laundry and supplies $3, and card fees are 2.9%. A client asked why color "costs so much" and I realized I couldn't actually say what we make on one. What do we make?

You can answer her with real numbers now. On one $85 color:

- Stylist commission: 45% of $85 = $38.25
- Product: $11.00
- Laundry and supplies: $3.00
- Card fees: 2.9% of $85 = $2.47
- Total direct cost: $54.72
- Left for the house: $85 − $54.72 = $30.28, a 35.6% contribution

That $30.28 is not profit yet — it still has to cover rent, utilities, the front desk, and your own pay. But it is a healthy contribution for a service that also fills the chair for other add-ons.

Two things worth noticing. First, commission is your biggest cost, not product — a $5 price rise adds $2.75 to the house after commission and card fees, while squeezing product cost by $1 adds exactly $1. Second, if you ever discount color by 10% (to $76.50), the house share falls to $25.86 — because commission and card fees shrink with the price, you give up about 15% of your contribution for that 10% cut. That is the math to remember before the next promotion.

My HVAC tech priced a coil job by taking our total cost of $950 and adding 40% because "our margin is 40%." I told him markup and margin aren't the same thing but I couldn't show him the difference on the actual job. Can you lay it out?

This is the most expensive vocabulary mix-up in the trades. Same job, same $950 cost, two different prices:

```
JOB COST: $950 (parts $640 + labor $310)

WHAT YOUR TECH DID — 40% MARKUP:
Price  = 950 x 1.40            = $1,330.00
Profit = 1,330 - 950           = $380.00
Margin = 380 / 1,330           = 28.6%   <-- not 40%

WHAT A 40% MARGIN ACTUALLY REQUIRES:
Price  = 950 / (1 - 0.40)      = $1,583.33
Profit = 1,583.33 - 950        = $633.33
Markup = 633.33 / 950          = 66.7%
```

The difference on this one job is $253.33. Do this across a year of installs and the "we charge 40%" shop is quietly running a 28.6% business.

The rule to tape to the wall: markup is profit divided by **cost**; margin is profit divided by **price**. Price is always the bigger number, so the same profit is always a smaller percentage of it. To price from a target margin, divide cost by (1 − margin). To convert the other way: a 40% markup is a 28.6% margin, and a 40% margin needs a 66.7% markup. Neither is wrong — but only one of them is the number you told your accountant you run.

I'm an electrician, sole owner, two helpers. Revenue last year was $286,000, expenses $201,000, so my books show $85,000 profit and I feel pretty good. My accountant says I'm fooling myself because I work in the field 30 hours a week and never counted my own labor. Is she right?

She is, and here is the test she is applying. Your $85,000 "profit" is really two things bundled together: your pay for working in the field, and whatever the business itself earns on top of that. Unbundle it by asking what it would cost to replace you.

A hired master electrician doing your field hours would cost about $95,000 a year fully loaded in most markets. Subtract that from the book profit:

$85,000 − $95,000 = −$10,000

That is the business's true profit: negative ten thousand. You are not earning $85,000 plus a business profit — you are earning $85,000 for a $95,000 job and subsidizing the difference out of a business that earns nothing. If you got hurt in January, the "profit" would vanish the day your replacement started.

To fix it on paper: you need prices that cover your $95,000 replacement cost AND a real margin. Say you target a 10% net margin on $286,000, which is $28,600. You are short $10,000 + $28,600 = $38,600, which is a 13.5% price increase across the board (38,600 / 286,000). That sounds large until you frame it correctly: you are not raising prices 13.5% to get rich, you are raising them so that your wage stops being the business's hidden subsidy.

We charge $89 for a standard house clean. A clean takes about 2.2 hours in the home, plus half an hour of paid drive time. Cleaners earn $17/hr, burden is 18%, supplies run $4.50 a clean and vehicle cost about $6.20. Are we actually making money?

Yes — but less than the $89 sticker suggests. Cost it per clean:

- Loaded wage: $17 × 1.18 = $20.06/hr
- Paid time per clean: 2.2 + 0.5 = 2.7 hours → labor $54.16
- Supplies: $4.50
- Vehicle: $6.20
- Total cost: $64.86
- Contribution: $89 − $64.86 = $24.14, a 27.1% margin

That $24.14 still has to cover your office, insurance, and booking software, so the true net is thinner — but the service itself is sound.

The number to watch is the drive time. Half an hour of driving is $10.03 of labor that produces nothing a customer can see. If routing improvements cut the average drive to 20 minutes, cost falls to $61.52 and the margin rises to 30.9% without touching the price. And notice what happens if a clean runs long — at 2.7 hours in the home instead of 2.2, cost climbs to $74.89 and the margin drops to 15.9%. Your profit lives in scheduling density and time discipline far more than in the $89.

My landscaping crew is three people: a lead at $24/hr and two laborers at $18/hr. Burden is 21%. Equipment and fuel run about $11.40 per crew-hour and the truck and trailer about $6.00. We bill $105 per crew-hour and I feel like we're busy but broke. What does a crew-hour actually cost, and what should it cost?

Busy but broke is exactly what this worksheet predicts:

```
CREW COST PER HOUR
Lead, loaded:        $24.00 x 1.21   = $29.04
Laborer, loaded:     $18.00 x 1.21   = $21.78  x 2 = $43.56
Crew labor                                     = $72.60
Equipment and fuel                             = $11.40
Truck and trailer                              = $ 6.00
TRUE CREW COST PER HOUR                        = $90.00

At your $105 rate:  margin = (105 - 90) / 105  = 14.3%
Rate for a 25% margin: 90 / (1 - 0.25)         = $120.00
```

A 14.3% margin sounds survivable until one rainy week, one broken mower, or one callback eats it — those all come out of the same 14.3%. It also means a 10% "neighbor discount" takes your margin to under 5%: at $94.50 you keep $4.50 an hour.

Notice the crew math cuts the other way too. Adding a fourth laborer raises crew cost by $21.78/hr, so the rate only works if the bigger crew finishes jobs at least 24% faster. Crew size is a pricing decision, not just a scheduling one. Either bill $120, shrink the standard crew, or find the hours — but $105 against a $90 cost is a slow leak, not a business.

I detail cars solo. My interior detail is $119 and I figured I clear about $60 on it. A buddy asked what my actual costs are and I had to guess. Labor is me — say my time is worth $21/hr loaded. A detail takes about 3 hours on a typical car, supplies run $12.10, and I figure overhead is about $9 a car. What do I really clear?

You clear $34.90, not $60 — and the gap is almost entirely the third hour.

- Your time: 3 hrs × $21 = $63.00
- Supplies: $12.10
- Overhead share: $9.00
- Total cost: $84.10
- Profit: $119 − $84.10 = $34.90, a 29.3% margin

Your $60 estimate probably came from timing a clean, easy car at 2 hours ($42 of labor) and forgetting overhead. The typical car takes 3. That single hour is $21 of the $25 gap.

This is good news, actually: 29.3% is a workable margin, and now you know where it leaks. Two honest options. Price the reality — at $134 the same job earns a 37.2% margin. Or time-box the service: define the interior detail as up to 2.5 hours with a stated per-half-hour rate beyond that, so the trashed minivan stops costing the same as the tidy sedan. What you cannot do is keep discovering the third hour for free.

I cater events and price the food portion by marking my food cost up 35%. Last event: food cost $18.50 per guest, 120 guests. My business coach says I'm not actually making a 35% margin and it's costing me real money. Show me.

Your coach is right, and on a 120-guest event the confusion is worth over $400:

```
FOOD COST PER GUEST: $18.50

YOUR METHOD — 35% MARKUP:
Price per guest  = 18.50 x 1.35        = $24.98
Profit per guest = 24.98 - 18.50       = $ 6.48
Actual margin    = 6.48 / 24.98        = 25.9%

A TRUE 35% MARGIN:
Price per guest  = 18.50 / (1 - 0.35)  = $28.46
Profit per guest = 28.46 - 18.50       = $ 9.96

Difference: $3.49 per guest x 120 guests = $418.38 per event
```

Markup divides profit by cost; margin divides profit by price. Because price is the larger number, a 35% markup quietly becomes a 25.9% margin. Cater ten events like this a year and you have left roughly $4,200 on the table while believing you were protected.

The fix is one formula: when you want margin M, price = cost / (1 − M). And when a client negotiates, negotiate from the margin version — if you "meet them halfway" from the markup price, you are conceding from a number that was already 9 points thinner than you thought.

I run a wellness studio with massage (450 room-hours a month, $27,000 revenue) and float tanks (150 room-hours, $18,000 revenue). Shared overhead is $6,300 a month. My bookkeeper allocates overhead by revenue; my partner says allocate by hours. Does it actually change anything, or is this an accounting food fight?

It changes which service looks profitable — by $945 a month. Both methods split the same $6,300; they just tell different stories:

```
                    BY HOURS (600 total hrs)   BY REVENUE ($45,000 total)
Massage share       450/600 = 75%  -> $4,725              27/45 = 60% -> $3,780
Float share         150/600 = 25%  -> $1,575              18/45 = 40% -> $2,520
Float overhead/hr   1,575 / 150    = $10.50               2,520 / 150  = $16.80
```

Under revenue allocation, the float tanks carry $6.30 more overhead per hour — enough to flip a thin float service from "fine" to "loser" on paper, and enough to make massage look artificially cheap to discount.

Neither method is truth; each is a lens. The right question is what *drives* the cost. Rent and utilities are driven by space and hours, so hours is the more honest allocation for those. Marketing spend, though, really is driven by revenue goals, and card fees follow revenue exactly. The grown-up answer is to split the $6,300 into pools — space costs by hours, transaction costs by revenue — instead of fighting over one blunt ratio. But if you must pick one: allocate by the driver, not by whichever method makes your favorite service look good.
I pay my shop assistant $22/hr. When I quote jobs I use $22 as my labor cost because that's the wage. My brother-in-law, who runs a warehouse, says my real labor cost is closer to $30. Who's right?

Your brother-in-law is. The wage is just the first layer of what an hour of her work costs you:

```
TRUE COST OF ONE HOUR AT A $22 WAGE
Wage                              $22.00
Payroll taxes (FICA 7.65%)        $ 1.68
Workers' comp (6.2%)              $ 1.36
Unemployment insurance (eff.)     $ 0.94
Health insurance contribution     $ 2.85
Paid time off accrual (5%)        $ 1.10
Total burden                      $ 7.93   (36.0% on top of the wage)
LOADED COST PER HOUR              $29.93
```

Every job you quoted at $22/hr labor was underpriced by $7.93 an hour before overhead even entered the picture. On a 6-hour job that is $47.58 of cost you planned to absorb yourself.

Two habits fix this permanently. First, compute your burden rate once a year — add up everything you pay *because she exists as an employee*, divide by wages, and use the loaded rate everywhere. Second, when you give a raise, re-run it: a $1/hr raise at a 36% burden rate is really $1.36/hr, which is exactly the kind of thing worth knowing before you promise it in December and price it in January.

My bookkeeper says I have a pricing problem disguised as a lifestyle problem. I set my rates years ago when I needed $52,000 a year to live on. Now I need $78,000. Shop revenue is about $390,000. She says my prices have to move even though my costs haven't. Is that real?

It is real, and her framing is exactly right. Your labor rate has always contained your pay — when the pay you need rises, the rate has to rise, or the difference comes out of the business's margin one quiet month at a time.

The arithmetic is simple: you need $78,000 − $52,000 = $26,000 more per year out of the same shop. On $390,000 of revenue, that is a 6.7% price increase (26,000 / 390,000) just to fund your own raise — before any cost inflation, before any extra profit.

Notice what happens if you don't do it. The business doesn't send you a memo; it just gets slightly worse. You defer the truck replacement, skip the software upgrade, let the contingency fund sit empty. Two years later you have a shop that looks busy and an owner who is burned out and underpaid, and the eventual correction is a 15% jump instead of two 3.5% ones.

Owners resist this because a raise for yourself feels optional in a way that a supplier's increase doesn't. It isn't. Your pay is a cost of the business like rent — price it in, in small regular steps, the way you'd want a landlord to treat you.

I keep hearing that my techs' "utilization" is why we're not profitable. We have one tech: paid 40 hours a week at a loaded $31/hr. In a typical week he bills 26 hours. Overhead runs $780 a week. We charge $85/hr. Walk me through what utilization is doing to us.

Here is your whole profitability problem in one table:

```
WEEKLY COSTS (fixed):  labor 40 hrs x $31 = $1,240  +  overhead $780  = $2,020

AT 26 BILLABLE HOURS (today):
Labor per billable hr:   1,240 / 26 = $47.69
Overhead per bill. hr:     780 / 26 = $30.00
True cost per billable hr:            $77.69
Margin at $85: (85 - 77.69) / 85    =  8.6%

AT 30 BILLABLE HOURS:
Labor per billable hr:   1,240 / 30 = $41.33
Overhead per bill. hr:     780 / 30 = $26.00
True cost per billable hr:            $67.33
Margin at $85: (85 - 67.33) / 85    = 20.8%
```

Nothing about your price or your costs changed between those two columns. Four more billable hours a week — one per day, roughly — takes the margin from 8.6% to 20.8%, because every fixed dollar gets spread across more sold hours.

That is why utilization is a pricing input, not just an operations metric: your $85 rate was probably set imagining 32–34 billable hours. At 26, the rate is simply wrong for the business you actually run. You have three levers — raise the rate toward $98 (the price that earns that same 20.8% margin at 26 hours), raise utilization with tighter scheduling and fewer windshield hours, or some of each. What doesn't work is holding the price, holding the schedule, and hoping volume saves you.
I charge a flat $25 trip fee on every service call. A customer 26 miles round-trip away complained it was steep, and honestly I just made the number up years ago. What does a trip actually cost me?

Let's build your truck's real per-mile cost:

- Fuel: $0.21/mile
- Maintenance and tires: $0.14/mile
- Depreciation: $0.18/mile
- Insurance share: $0.07/mile
- Total: $0.60/mile

A 26-mile round trip is $15.60 of vehicle cost. But the truck isn't the expensive part — the driver is. Thirty-five minutes of driving at a loaded $44/hr is $25.67 of labor producing nothing billable. True dispatch cost for that call: $15.60 + $25.67 = $41.27.

So your made-up $25 fee undercharges that customer by about $16 — and, more importantly, it treats a 4-mile call and a 26-mile call as the same product, which quietly taxes your close-in customers to subsidize the far ones. Most shops land on one of two honest structures: a higher flat fee that reflects the average trip (yours would need to be around $41 just to break even on dispatch), or a modest base fee inside a stated radius with a per-mile or zone charge beyond it. Either is defensible to the customer who complained, because you can show her the $0.60 and the clock. What isn't defensible is a number from years ago that loses money on every long drive.

I give free estimates and I keep adding software to run my small contracting business: CRM $89/mo, estimating tool $59, accounting $45, phones $120, scheduling $99. It feels like death by a thousand cuts. How much is this stuff actually adding to each job? We do about 68 jobs a month and average $180 a job.

Add it up first: $89 + $59 + $45 + $120 + $99 = $412 a month. Spread over 68 jobs, that is $6.06 per job — about 3.4% of your $180 average ticket.

That framing does two things. First, it tells you the software stack is not your problem: $6.06 a job is a rounding error next to one underestimated labor hour. Second, it tells you where the money actually goes — your "free" estimates. If you write 90 estimates a month at 40 minutes each, that is 60 hours of skilled time producing the 68 jobs you won and 22 expensive pieces of paper. The estimating software is the cheapest part of estimating.

None of this means keep every subscription. It means audit them the right way: per job, not per month. A tool that costs $6.06 a job and saves ten minutes of office time per job is paying for itself several times over. A tool nobody opens is $59 of pure overhead. And when you set next year's prices, that $412 belongs in the overhead pool your rates are built on — it is a real cost of delivering a job, just one that arrives by autopay instead of by invoice.

I have a deck repair job: materials $1,150, labor $860, disposal $90. I want to actually clear a 25% net margin on it. My usual method is to add 25% on top of cost. What should I quote, and what does my usual method really give me?

Your total cost is $1,150 + $860 + $90 = $2,100. Now watch the two methods diverge:

```
TARGET: 25% MARGIN (profit = 25% of the PRICE)

Correct method:  price = cost / (1 - margin)
                 price = 2,100 / 0.75        = $2,800.00
                 profit = 2,800 - 2,100      = $  700.00
                 check: 700 / 2,800          = 25.0% ✓

Your usual method: 25% MARKUP
                 price = 2,100 x 1.25        = $2,625.00
                 profit = 2,625 - 2,100      = $  525.00
                 actual margin: 525 / 2,625  = 20.0%
```

Quote $2,800. Your usual method leaves $175 on this job and, more subtly, trains you to believe you run a 25% business while running a 20% one — a gap that shows up at year-end as a mystery.

The conversion worth memorizing: to earn margin M, multiply cost by 1 / (1 − M). For 25% that multiplier is 1.333, not 1.25. For 30% it is 1.429; for 20% it is 1.25 — which is why your method felt right: adding 25% genuinely does produce a 20% margin. If 20% is honestly enough, keep the method and rename the target. Just stop calling it 25%.

A homeowner showed me two competing bids for her bathroom tile job: $3,350 and $2,600. Mine is $4,200. My costs: materials $1,480 (proper membrane, mid-grade tile), labor 34 hours at a loaded $58/hr... wait, labor is in there — let me just say my price is built from real costs. She asked why the low bid is so low. I don't want to badmouth anyone; I want to show her the arithmetic. Help me reconstruct what a $2,600 bid has to leave out.

You don't need to say a word about the other contractor. Just do the subtraction out loud:

```
YOUR PRICE: $4,200
Materials (tile, membrane, setting materials): $1,480
Labor: 34 hrs x $58 loaded = $1,972, plus overhead and profit

THE $2,600 BID, RECONSTRUCTED TWO WAYS:

Option 1 — same materials:
  2,600 - 1,480 = $1,120 left for ALL labor, overhead, and profit
  $1,120 / $58 = 19.3 hours of labor — for a 34-hour job
  Something is not being done. The usual candidate: the
  waterproofing membrane ($310 of materials + ~4 hours),
  or prep and leveling.

Option 2 — cheaper materials ($890, no membrane, budget tile):
  2,600 - 890 = $1,710 for labor and everything else
  = 29.5 hours at $58 — still short of 34, with zero profit
  and zero overhead recovery built in.
```

Either way, the bid only balances if scope disappears, labor is paid far below a legal loaded rate, or the plan is to find the missing money later in change orders. Tile is the worst place in the house for that discovery: a failed shower floor costs more to tear out and redo than the original job, and the membrane is the part you cannot inspect once the tile is on.

Give the homeowner the two questions that cost her nothing to ask: "Is waterproofing membrane included, in writing? And is this price fixed, or an estimate?" Her contractor's answers will tell her which reconstruction she's holding.

I keep going back and forth: flat-rate pricing or time-and-materials for water heater replacements? My flat price is $1,850. Average job: parts $920, labor 3.2 hours at a loaded $62/hr, overhead allocation $192. About 1 job in 8 hits corroded lines and adds $260 of cost. Run the numbers from my side of the counter.

From your side, flat-rate wins this one — here is why, with the bad jobs included:

```
FLAT RATE AT $1,850:
Average job cost: 920 + (3.2 x 62) + 192        = $1,310.40
Margin on a normal job: (1850 - 1310.40) / 1850 = 29.2%
Expected corrosion cost: $260 / 8 jobs          = $32.50 per job
Risk-adjusted cost:                               $1,342.90
Risk-adjusted margin:                             27.4%

TIME-AND-MATERIALS EQUIVALENT:
Parts at 1.35 markup: 920 x 1.35                = $1,242.00
Labor: 3.2 hrs x $110                           = $  352.00
Typical ticket:                                   $1,594.00
```

T&M looks safer because every job covers its own costs, but look at what it gives up: the efficient jobs earn the same rate as the disasters, customers watch the clock and dispute the hours, and your best tech — the one who finishes in 2.6 hours — literally earns you less money. Flat-rate flips that: speed becomes profit, the customer buys certainty, and the 1-in-8 corrosion job is just a $32.50 insurance premium spread across every ticket.

The discipline flat-rate demands: your average cost has to be *true*. If real labor is 3.9 hours, not 3.2, your risk-adjusted margin is 25.1%, not 27.4% — still fine, but only if you know it. Re-cost the flat price from actual job data every year, and keep a stated exception for genuine surprises (a failed shutoff valve is not "corrosion"), quoted before work continues.

I'm the customer this time. My appliance repair company quoted two ways to fix my dryer: time-and-materials ($89 diagnostic, $95/hr labor, parts extra — they estimate 1.5 hours and about $60 in parts) or a flat $329 all-in. Which is the smarter buy?

Price both futures, not just the expected one.

Time-and-materials, if the estimate holds: $89 + (1.5 × $95) + $60 = $291.50. You save $37.50 versus the flat quote.

Time-and-materials, if the job fights back — a second fault found, 3 hours total: $89 + (3 × $95) + $60 = $434. Now the flat quote would have saved you $105.

So the $329 flat price is really an insurance policy with a $37.50 premium: you pay $37.50 more than the expected T&M bill in exchange for capping your worst case $105 below the bad-luck outcome. Whether that's smart depends on two things. First, how much you trust the 1.5-hour estimate — dryers are usually honest, quick diagnoses, which argues for T&M. Second, whether a $434 surprise would actually hurt; if it just annoys you, self-insure and take T&M.

One question sharpens the decision: ask whether the $89 diagnostic is credited toward the repair under each option. If it's credited under the flat quote but not under T&M, the flat price's real premium shrinks — and companies know exactly which structure makes the diagnostic disappear. Get that in writing before you choose.

I'm quoting a deck build: materials $6,840, labor 64 hours at a loaded $47/hr, permits and dump fees $410. I want a 30% margin on the job. What do I quote, and what markup does that work out to? (My partner swears the answer is "just add 30%.")

Your partner's method would underquote this job by over $1,300. Build it properly:

- Materials: $6,840
- Labor: 64 × $47 = $3,008
- Permits and disposal: $410
- Total cost: $10,258

For a 30% margin, price = cost / (1 − 0.30) = 10,258 / 0.70 = $14,654.29. Quote $14,650.

The markup equivalent: ($14,654.29 − $10,258) / $10,258 = 42.9%. That is the number that surprises everyone — a 30% margin *is* a 42.9% markup, because margin divides by the bigger number (price) and markup by the smaller (cost).

If you had "just added 30%," the quote would be $13,335.40, and your actual margin would be ($13,335.40 − $10,258) / $13,335.40 = 23.1%. On one deck that's a $1,319 lesson. Across a season of builds it's the difference between a business that funds its own equipment and one that wonders where the money went.

Give your partner the converter and tape it to the estimating desk: margin 20% = markup 25%; margin 25% = markup 33.3%; margin 30% = markup 42.9%; margin 40% = markup 66.7%.

We just raised our minimum service charge to $129 and a longtime customer called it gouging. It's for a call that might only take 20 minutes of actual work. How do I know $129 isn't just greed — and how would I explain it?

Run the cost of the smallest possible call, using your own numbers (loaded labor $58/hr):

- Drive time, 24 minutes average: 0.4 × $58 = $23.20
- First half hour of labor on site: 0.5 × $58 = $29.00
- Dispatch and office handling: $11.00
- Vehicle cost for the trip: $9.40
- Floor cost of the call: $72.60

Your old minimum — $79, if yours was like most shops — earned $6.40 over that floor, an 8.1% margin, before a single callback. One free return visit erased the profit on roughly ten minimum calls. At $129 you keep $56.40, a 43.7% margin on the smallest tickets — healthy, and it has to be, because short calls carry the same fixed dispatch cost as long ones with a fraction of the billable time to spread it over.

The explanation to the customer writes itself once you see it this way: "The $129 isn't for 20 minutes of work. It's for getting a stocked truck and a licensed tech to your door — the drive, the dispatch, and the first half hour are the same whether the fix takes 20 minutes or 50." People accept minimums they can see the shape of. What they call gouging is usually just a number nobody ever explained.

We charge a $119 diagnostic fee for appliance calls, credited toward the repair if the customer goes ahead. About 68% of customers proceed with the repair. A competitor charges no diagnostic fee at all and advertises it hard. Is our fee costing us, or is the structure actually sound?

The structure is sound — it's a filter that pays for itself. Look at the 32% who don't proceed. Without a fee, those visits are pure cost: a diagnostic trip runs about $64 in tech time, vehicle, and dispatch. With the credited fee, a non-repair visit brings in $119 against that $64 cost — a 46.2% margin on the visits your competitor does for free.

And the credit is doing quiet psychological work. Once a customer has $119 "in the job," the repair quote is judged against the remaining balance, not the full price — your close rate on the repair itself is higher than the no-fee shop's, because their customers face the entire amount as one decision.

Where the fee genuinely costs you is the phone call, not the visit: some callers won't book at all. The defense is how you frame it — "the $119 includes the trip, the diagnosis, and a firm quote, and it comes off the repair if you go ahead." That sentence converts the fee from a toll into a deposit. Your competitor's "free diagnostic" is being paid for somewhere: either his repair prices carry it, or his techs are rushed into shallower diagnoses. You don't need to say that. Just keep your close rate and your non-repair margin where they are, and let him advertise.

Every gutter cleaner in my area charges $249 for a standard house, so that's the market price whether I like it or not. I want a 30% margin. My crew costs $78/hr loaded (two techs), plus $21 of vehicle and dispatch per job. A standard house takes 1.6 hours, but the big two-stories take 2.1. Does the market price even work for me?

Work backward from the price — this is called target costing, and it's the right way to handle a price the market hands you:

```
MARKET PRICE: $249   TARGET MARGIN: 30%
Allowable total cost: 249 x (1 - 0.30)        = $174.30

STANDARD HOUSE (1.6 hrs):
  Labor 1.6 x $78 = $124.80  +  $21 dispatch  = $145.80
  Headroom vs allowable: 174.30 - 145.80      = $ 28.50  ✓ works

BIG TWO-STORY (2.1 hrs):
  Labor 2.1 x $78 = $163.80  +  $21 dispatch  = $184.80
  vs allowable $174.30                        = $ 10.50 OVER ✗
```

So the market price works beautifully on the standard house and quietly loses money on the big ones — at $249, a 2.1-hour job runs a 25.8% margin *before* anything goes wrong, and below 30% by design. The fix isn't to abandon $249; it's to stop pretending one price covers both houses. Keep $249 as the advertised standard (up to a stated size or single-story), and price the big two-stories at $289 — which restores the target: (289 − 184.80) / 289 = 36.1%, giving you room to land at $269 in a negotiation and still clear 31%.

The general discipline: when the market sets the price, your job is to find the cost line it can support, then draw your service boundaries exactly where the math breaks — not where it gets awkward to explain.

Half my moving jobs need two people, half can be done solo, but I've been quoting one blended hourly rate. Lead mover costs me $34.50/hr loaded, a helper $23.75, truck and equipment about $13/hr while we're on a job. What should the two-person rate actually be if I want a 28% margin? Right now it's $85 and it feels thin.

Your instinct is right — $85 is thin. Build the two-person crew rate from its parts:

- Lead, loaded: $34.50
- Helper, loaded: $23.75
- Truck and equipment: $13.00
- True crew cost: $71.25/hr
- Price for a 28% margin: 71.25 / (1 − 0.28) = $98.96 → quote $99/hr

At your current $85, the margin is (85 − 71.25) / 85 = 16.2%. On a 5-hour two-person move that's $68.75 of profit for a day of heavy liability — one scratched floor consumes it.

The blended rate is the deeper problem. When a solo job gets quoted at the blended rate, you're either overcharging the easy work (and losing those bids) or undercharging the crew work (and winning bids that lose money). Moving has a clean fix because the crew size is knowable at booking: quote solo and two-person rates separately, and let the job survey decide which applies. Customers accept a crew rate without blinking when it's stated up front — what they fight is a rate that changes mid-job. Publish both, hold both, and let the $99 do the work the blended $85 couldn't.

I do kitchen remodels and I price the whole job at one blended margin. A friend who does bigger jobs prices materials and labor at different margins — materials at 20%, labor at 35%. On a job with $9,600 of materials cost and $7,300 of labor cost, what does her structure produce versus my flat approach? I usually aim for about 25% overall.

Different margins for materials and labor isn't fussiness — it reflects that the two costs behave differently. Watch what her structure does to your job:

```
HER STRUCTURE:
Materials: 9,600 / (1 - 0.20)   = $12,000.00
Labor:     7,300 / (1 - 0.35)   = $11,230.77
Quote total:                      $23,230.77
Total cost:                       $16,900.00
Blended margin: 6,330.77 / 23,230.77 = 27.3%

YOUR FLAT 25%:
16,900 / (1 - 0.25)             = $22,533.33
```

Her quote is $697 higher and her blended margin is 27.3% versus your 25% — but the real difference is *where* the profit sits. Labor is where remodels bleed: overruns, callbacks, and your own underestimation all land on labor hours, never on the tile invoice. Pricing labor at 35% builds the shock absorber exactly where the shocks arrive. Materials, meanwhile, are pass-through-ish — the client can price-check a faucet in thirty seconds, so a fat materials margin is the one most likely to get shopped and lost.

The reverse warning also applies: if your jobs are materials-heavy (high-end appliances, stone), a labor-weighted structure underprices the risk of a cracked $4,000 slab. Match the margin to where the risk and the invisibility are. Labor is both riskier and harder for clients to comparison-shop — that's the whole argument.

My service manager says we should build warranty and callback costs into our prices instead of eating them. We run about 1,150 jobs a year, average ticket $310. Roughly 4% of jobs need a free return visit costing us about $138, and about 1.5% have a parts failure under warranty costing about $210. How much belongs in each ticket?

This is just insurance mathematics — spread the expected cost across every job instead of letting it ambush individual ones:

```
EXPECTED WARRANTY COST PER JOB:
Callbacks:      4.0% x $138   = $5.52
Parts failures: 1.5% x $210   = $3.15
Reserve per ticket:             $8.67

Annual view: 1,150 jobs x $8.67 = $9,970.50
As a share of the $310 ticket: 2.8%
```

So roughly $9 added to every ticket — or a 2.8% bump to the rate card — fully funds your warranty exposure. Right now you're paying that same $9,970.50 anyway; you're just paying it out of margin, invisibly, and feeling vaguely unprofitable in the months when callbacks cluster.

Two refinements once the reserve exists. First, track the actuals against the 4% and 1.5% assumptions quarterly — if callbacks creep to 6%, the reserve goes to $11.43 and you want to know whether that's a pricing problem or a training problem (usually it's one tech, and it's a training problem). Second, never let the reserve become a reason to shrug at callbacks. The money being budgeted doesn't make a return visit free — the customer still spent their Saturday waiting for you twice. The reserve protects the P&L; the callback rate still owns your reputation.

We're a plumbing shop and jobs keep landing farther out. Inside our normal area we're fine, but some calls are 18 extra miles round-trip beyond our usual radius and take about 26 extra minutes of driving. Truck cost is about $0.58/mile and my tech's loaded rate is $49/hr. What should a distance surcharge actually be?

Price the trip, not the guilt:

- Extra vehicle cost: 18 miles × $0.58 = $10.44
- Extra drive time: 26 minutes × $49/hr = $21.23
- True extra cost: $31.67

So a $35 surcharge beyond your standard radius covers the real cost with a small cushion; anything under about $32 is a donation. Notice the split — the driving *time* costs twice what the driving itself does. That's true for almost every trade, and it's why per-mile-only surcharges always feel too small.

Structure matters as much as size. State the radius in the booking call ("our standard area runs to about 20 miles; beyond that there's a $35 travel charge"), because a surcharge disclosed up front is a policy and the same surcharge discovered on the invoice is a fight. And build the escape hatch: if three jobs cluster in the far area on one day, waive or split the surcharge — the math that justified it (a dedicated long trip) no longer applies when the truck is already there. Customers remember that kind of fairness, and it costs you nothing you were actually spending.

I want to add a scalp-treatment add-on at my salon but have no idea what to charge for something brand new. Product cost is $6, it takes my stylist about 20 minutes (her loaded cost is $28/hr), and I figure chair overhead at $4. Where do I even start?

Start from cost, then treat the first price as an experiment with a review date:

- Product: $6.00
- Stylist time: 20 min × $28/hr = $9.33
- Chair overhead: $4.00
- Total cost: $19.33

A launch price of $39 gives you a 50.4% margin — (39 − 19.33) / 39 — which is the right neighborhood for an add-on, because add-ons should be your highest-margin work: they monetize a client who is already in the chair, with zero acquisition cost.

Then run it as a pilot, not a marriage. Offer it for 30 services and track two numbers: the take rate (how many clients say yes when offered) and the actual time it takes (services have a way of growing). If the take rate is under about 15%, the price is probably the friction — test $32, which still earns a 39.6% margin, before concluding nobody wants it. If stylists are offering it selectively because it runs long, that's a time problem wearing a price problem's clothes.

The mistake to avoid is launching at a "friendly" $24 to be safe. That earns a 19.5% margin, trains clients to value the service at $24, and leaves you no room to ever fix it. New services are the one place you can set the price with no history fighting you — spend that freedom on a real margin.

I quoted a kitchen job at $9,800 with a 26% margin, materials $3,900 of it, mostly lumber. The customer sat on the quote for 45 days, then accepted — and lumber had gone up 8% in the meantime. My quotes say "valid 30 days" but I honored it anyway to keep the relationship. What did that cost me, and how do I stop it happening again?

It cost you $312, and the margin math shows why it stings: your gross profit was 26% of $9,800 = $2,548. The lumber increase — 8% of $3,900 = $312 — comes straight out of that, leaving $2,236, a 22.8% margin. You didn't lose money; you donated about an eighth of the job's profit to a calendar.

The fix is to make the quote's validity real and mechanical, in two parts. First, shorten validity on materials-heavy quotes to 21 days, and say why at signing: "This price holds while the lumber package holds; after the 21st I'll re-price materials at cost and show you the invoice either way." Customers accept this readily when it's explained before there's a number to argue about — lumber volatility is news to no one.

Second, for accepted-but-delayed jobs, add an escalation clause with a threshold: materials repriced only if the package moves more than 3%, documented by supplier invoices. The threshold matters — it tells the customer you're not nickel-and-diming normal drift, and it tells your future self exactly when to have the conversation. Honoring the $9,800 once was a reasonable relationship investment. Honoring it as a habit is a 3-point margin leak with a smile on it.

I'm a barber booked out three weeks at $38 a cut, doing about 34 cuts a week. Everyone tells me to raise prices. If I go to $44, how do I think about what happens to volume? Someone mentioned "elasticity" and I nodded like I understood.

You nodded at the right concept — here's what it means with your numbers. Elasticity is just the ratio: how much volume moves when price moves. For a booked-out barber with loyal clients, a reasonable *guess* — and label it a guess, because nobody knows yours until you test it — is an elasticity of −0.4: a 10% price rise costs about 4% of volume.

Run your raise through it:

- Price: $38 → $44 is +15.8%
- Expected volume change: −0.4 × 15.8% ≈ −6.3%
- Cuts: 34 × 0.937 ≈ 31.9 per week
- Revenue: was 34 × $38 = $1,292/week; becomes ≈ 31.9 × $44 = $1,402/week

So revenue rises about 8.5% while you do two fewer cuts — roughly two hours a week handed back to you, or room for two new clients at the higher price. And here's the part the three-week waitlist tells you: right now you're turning people away, which means demand exceeds your supply at $38. A barber with a waitlist is underpriced almost by definition — the raise isn't a risk, it's a correction, and the first clients it "costs" you were ones you couldn't serve anyway.

If the guess is wrong and elasticity is really −0.8, you'd do about 29.7 cuts for $1,307 — still ahead. The raise only loses if volume falls more than 13.6%, and a three-week book says that's unlikely.

I run a cleaning company and January is dead — my crews are idle about 30% of their hours. I'm thinking of a January discount on deep cleans: normally $240, cost is about $138 in labor and supplies, and my cleaners are paid only for hours worked. Does discounting to fill January make sense, or am I training people to wait for sales?

It makes sense here, and the reason is in one phrase you said: *paid only for hours worked*. An idle January hour earns $0 and costs $0; a discounted clean converts that hour into contribution:

- At 15% off: price $204, cost $138, contribution $66 per clean
- Fill 14 extra cleans across the month: $924 of contribution that otherwise simply doesn't exist

That's the test for any fill-the-gap discount: is the capacity perishable and is the marginal cost truly avoided when idle? Your labor is, so yes. (If your crews were salaried, the same discount would need a different analysis — the labor cost would be sunk and the question becomes whether $204 beats the *supplies-only* marginal cost, which it does even more easily, but the discount would be funding work you'd pay for anyway.)

Now the guardrails, because your second fear is legitimate. Training happens when discounts are *predictable and universal*. Make this one neither: weekday mornings only, January dates only, new bookings only, announced to your existing list as a fixed block of slots. A client who shifts her deep clean from February to a January Tuesday morning is fine — you wanted exactly that. A client who learns "never book at full price" is the failure mode, and she learns it from standing sales, not from a bounded January fill. Keep the boundary bright and the discount is a tool; blur it and it becomes your price.

My grooming salon gets about 46 booking requests a week but we only have capacity for 38 appointments in our 36 open hours. There's a permanent waitlist and my staff are burning out. Everyone says "just raise prices," but how much would price alone actually have to do? Assume demand responds with an elasticity around -0.5.

Let's make price do the math in public, because "just raise prices" usually fails this test:

```
THE GAP:
Requests: 46/wk    Capacity: 38/wk    Demand must fall: 17.4%

PRICE ALONE (elasticity -0.5):
Required price rise = 17.4% / 0.5 = +34.8%
A 35% jump, all at once, on loyal customers — unrealistic
and it would torch goodwill long before it balanced the book.

THE COMBINATION THAT WORKS:
Price +12%:  demand -6%  -> 46 x 0.94 = 43.2 requests
Add 4 hours (one evening): capacity 38 + ~4.2 slots = 42.2
Remaining overflow: about 1 request/wk — a healthy waitlist
```

A waitlist of one is a business asset — it fills cancellations and proves demand. A waitlist of eight is a leak: those clients eventually book elsewhere and don't come back.

Two warnings from the numbers. First, the −0.5 elasticity is an assumption, not a measurement; if your clients are less price-sensitive (say −0.3), the same 12% raise only trims demand to 44.3, and you still need the hours. Treat the first raise as an experiment and watch the request count weekly. Second, notice what this analysis says about your real problem: at current prices you are a 42-slot business wearing a 38-slot schedule. Sometimes the honest answer to "raise prices or add capacity?" is a measured amount of both — price rations the demand you can't serve, hours serve the demand you can.

My salon's Tuesdays are empty (about 45% chair utilization) while Saturdays run at 98%. I'm considering 20% off color on Tuesdays only — color is $120, direct cost about $51. My fear: my Saturday clients will just move to Tuesday and I'll lose money on people who'd have paid full price. Talk me through it.

Your fear has a name — cannibalization — and it can be priced. First, the Tuesday math on its own:

- Tuesday color at 20% off: $96
- Direct cost: $51
- Contribution per Tuesday booking: $45, versus $0 for an empty chair

Now your scenario, with honest numbers. Suppose the offer produces 10 Tuesday color bookings a week, and 2 of them are Saturday clients who moved. The movers cost you the discount on work you'd have sold anyway: 2 × $24 = $48. The other 8 are genuinely new contribution: 8 × $45 = $360. Net: +$312 a week.

But wait — one detail in your own numbers softens the fear further. Saturday is at 98%: a client who moves to Tuesday frees a Saturday slot that your waitlist likely refills at full price. The mover only truly costs you if her Saturday slot goes empty, and at 98% utilization it almost never does.

The real risk isn't the mover; it's the *message*. If "Tuesday discount" becomes a permanent feature, some clients reorganize their whole habit around it. Keep it as a stated, bounded program ("Tuesday color special, through the end of the quarter"), review the Saturday refill rate monthly, and the discount stays a tool for filling dead chairs rather than a slow re-pricing of your whole week.

I'm a wedding photographer. I have 22 prime Saturdays a year and got 31 inquiries for them last season. My package is $2,900 regardless of day. Costs per wedding are about $1,150 (second shooter, editing time, album). A mentor says Saturdays should cost more. Is that just greed, or is there actual math?

There's actual math, and it starts with a number you already have: 31 inquiries, 22 Saturdays. Nine couples will be told no no matter what you charge:

```
CURRENT (any day $2,900):
Margin: (2,900 - 1,150) / 2,900 = 60.3%
You book all 22 Saturdays early — often by the couples
who inquired first, not the ones who value the date most.

SATURDAY AT $3,600 (+24.1%):
Margin: (3,600 - 1,150) / 3,600 = 68.1%
Season difference if all 22 book: 22 x $700 = $15,400
```

The principle is opportunity cost. A Saturday sold at $2,900 doesn't cost you $1,150 — it costs you $1,150 *plus the other booking that Saturday can never take again*. There are 22 of these slots a year, ever. A Tuesday wedding, by contrast, displaces nothing; your calendar is empty, so $2,900 on a Tuesday is nearly pure gain. Same work, same cost, genuinely different product — because one of them is scarce.

This is also why the premium isn't greed in any sense that matters: you disclose it up front, couples who care most about the date pay it, couples who are flexible get rewarded with the weekday price, and nobody is surprised at the invoice. Rationing a scarce slot by price is how the slot goes to the couple who values it most. Rationing by "who emailed first in January" is not more virtuous — it's just less honest about what's being allocated.

I detail cars. My basic wash is $59 and it attracts the most price-sensitive customers I have — they use about 40% of my slots but the margin on a wash is only about $11 after costs. My full detail is $149 with a $61 margin. I'm thinking of raising the wash to $79 to shed some of that work. My partner says losing customers is always bad. Is it?

Losing *these* customers, at *these* margins, is arithmetic, not failure. Run your own numbers on 10 wash slots a week:

Today: 10 washes × $11 margin = $110 of weekly profit from those slots, and your detail bays' schedule is clogged with the lowest-value work you sell.

After the raise to $79: suppose 6 of the 10 wash customers leave (they were only ever buying a price), 4 stay. If just 4 of the 6 freed slots refill with $149 details across the week:

4 × $11 + 4 × $61 = $44 + $244 = $288 — versus $110 today, with 2 slots still empty.

Even if only 2 slots refill with details: $44 + $122 = $166, still well ahead, and you're working less for it. The raise only loses if *zero* freed slots refill and all 6 customers walk — and even then you've traded $66 of thin margin for hours you can spend marketing the $61 work.

The principle generalizes: a customer is not a unit of good. A slot is a unit of capacity, and it earns whatever the work in it earns. When your lowest-margin service is also your most price-sensitive and most schedule-hungry, raising its price isn't arrogance — it's how you find out which of those customers valued *you* and which valued *$59*. Keep the ones who valued you. They were never the problem.

I run a mobile dog grooming van. I have exactly 6 Saturday slots and 11 regular clients who all want Saturdays. Weekdays have slack. I hate the idea of a "weekend premium" — it feels like punishing people for having jobs. Grooming is $95, my cost is about $52. What are my real options?

Your discomfort is understandable, but look at what you're doing now: rationing 6 slots among 11 people by *guilt and rotation* — which quietly punishes the clients who are least pushy. Price is just a more transparent rationing rule. The numbers:

- At $95: margin is (95 − 52) / 95 = 45.3%
- Saturday at $120: margin is (120 − 52) / 120 = 56.7%

But you have three options, and only one is a straight premium:

1. **Saturday premium (+$25).** The clients who truly need Saturday — the ones whose jobs you mentioned — reveal it by paying; the ones who were on Saturday by habit drift to weekdays, freeing slots. Nobody is punished; they're sorted by how much the day matters to them.

2. **Weekday incentive instead.** Saturday stays $95; weekday grooms go to $85 for clients who switch. Same sorting, framed as a reward. It costs you $10 on every weekday groom, including ones that were never competing for Saturday — usually the more expensive way to buy the same movement.

3. **Grandfather and rotate fairly.** Current Saturday regulars keep their slots at $95 for a set period; new Saturday demand pays the premium or takes weekdays.

Most groomers land on option 1 with a grandfather window from option 3. And one framing note for the client conversation: you're not charging for their job — you're charging for the slot eleven people want and six can have. That's a sentence most people accept, because it's visibly true.

I run a pool service. Spring openings I charge $289, fall closings $249, and the work is basically identical — same crew, same time, cost is about $141 either way. A customer who does both asked why spring costs more if the work is the same. I didn't have a good answer that wasn't "because I can." Is there one?

There is, and it's more respectable than "because I can": cost is the floor for a price, not the price itself. Your margins show the structure:

- Spring opening: (289 − 141) / 289 = 51.2% margin
- Fall closing: (249 − 141) / 249 = 43.4% margin

In spring, every pool owner in your area wants the same three weeks. Your crew's calendar is the scarce resource, and an opening slot sold cheap is a slot another customer would have paid full price for. In fall, demand is soft and spread out — the binding problem is keeping the crew busy, so the price leans toward filling hours. Same work, different scarcity, different price. Airlines and hotels run on exactly this logic and nobody accuses the Tuesday flight of being a scam.

The honest sentence for your customer: "The work is the same; the calendar isn't. In April I turn away openings every week, so the price reflects the slot. In October I'm competing to fill the route, so it comes down." Most customers accept seasonal pricing instantly when it's stated that plainly — what they resent is suspecting the number was invented for them personally. A published seasonal schedule, same for everyone, solves that too.

I'm a massage therapist and tomorrow has two empty slots that will just evaporate. I have a text list of about 84 past clients. A friend suggested blasting a "tomorrow only, 20% off" offer. My regular price is $95, and since I'm paid per session, my cost on a session is about $37 (my pay share plus laundry). Good idea or slippery slope?

Good idea, with one design rule. The economics first:

- Discounted price: $95 × 0.80 = $76
- Your cost: $37
- Contribution per filled slot: $39 — versus $0 for the slot evaporating

At a typical 3% response rate, 84 texts produce about 2.5 replies — usually enough to fill both slots, converting a dead afternoon into roughly $78 of contribution. This is the cleanest case in all of discounting: the inventory is perishable (tomorrow's 2pm cannot be sold on Wednesday), the marginal cost is low and real, and the discount applies only to the units that would otherwise be wasted.

The slippery slope is *predictability*. If clients learn that Friday afternoons always get a Thursday text, some full-price Friday bookings quietly migrate to "wait for the text" bookings, and you've re-priced your week. So: send it only for genuine, irregular gaps; never on a rhythm; never two weeks in a row; and always tie it to the specific slots ("tomorrow, the 2:00 and 4:00 just opened"). Scarcity that is visibly real doesn't train anyone — it just fills a chair that was going to sit empty, at a price that still respects your costs.

I run a dog daycare, 40 spots a day, currently full with a waitlist of about 6 dogs. Day rate is $46 and I'm considering $52. Everyone has an opinion on how many customers I'll lose. How do I think about this without just guessing?

You can't avoid guessing — but you can guess in scenarios instead of in arguments. Elasticity (how much volume a price rise costs) is unknown, so price the decision at three values of it. Your rise is +13.0% ($46 → $52):

```
SCENARIO TABLE (expected dogs/day, revenue/day)
Today:                              40 dogs    $1,840

Elasticity -0.2 (loyal clientele):
  Volume -2.6%  -> 39.0 dogs        $2,026     +10.1%
Elasticity -0.5 (average sensitivity):
  Volume -6.5%  -> 37.4 dogs        $1,945      +5.7%
Elasticity -1.0 (very sensitive):
  Volume -13.0% -> 34.8 dogs        $1,810      -1.6%
```

Now the detail everyone forgets: you have a 6-dog waitlist. Demand has to fall past the waitlist before a single spot actually empties — the first ~15% of "lost" demand is absorbed by people who already want in. So even the harsh scenario likely runs at a full house for months, at $52 × 40 = $2,080 a day, while the waitlist slowly drains and tells you the truth about your elasticity.

That makes this close to a free experiment: raise the rate, watch the waitlist length weekly. If it holds, the market has answered. If it drains to zero and spots start opening, you have measured your real elasticity — information worth money all by itself — and you can adjust from knowledge instead of from fear.

My HVAC shop is at capacity every summer — we turn away work June through August. Seasonal revenue is about $486,000 at current prices. Two options: raise prices 8% (my guess is we'd lose about 3% of volume), or add a fourth tech for the season. A seasonal tech costs $31/hr loaded, 40 hrs a week for 13 weeks, plus $4,300 for truck and equipment. Added billable work would be about 62% of his hours at our $118/hr billing rate, with materials on that work running about $9,880. Which wins?

Run both options to the same finish line — incremental profit:

```
OPTION A — RAISE PRICES 8% (volume -3%, your guess):
New revenue: 486,000 x 1.08 x 0.97 = $509,134
Gain: +$23,134, with zero added cost and zero added risk

OPTION B — ADD A SEASONAL TECH:
Added billable hours: 520 hrs x 62%        = 322.4
Added revenue: 322.4 x $118                = $38,043
Less tech labor: 520 x $31                 = -$16,120
Less materials:                            = -$ 9,880
Less truck and equipment:                  = -$ 4,300
Gain:                                        +$7,743
```

Option A wins by about $15,400 — *if* your volume guess holds. So find the breaking point: the price rise matches today's revenue if volume falls 7.4% (since 1.08 × 0.926 = 1.00). Your guess is 3%. The raise only becomes the wrong choice if the true volume loss is more than double your estimate — possible, but that's a wide safety margin, and a shop turning away work all summer is, almost by definition, priced below what its market will bear.

Option B has one thing A doesn't: it builds capacity and a possible full-time hire. If your constraint is really a labor shortage you expect to persist, B is an investment, not just a seasonal play. But as a pure summer-profit decision, the price rise does more with less — and it fixes the underlying issue, which is that turned-away customers were telling you the price was wrong.

I run a seasonal boat detailing business — basically May through September. Annual fixed costs are $61,200 (storage, insurance, base expenses) and I need $24,000 of profit to make the year work. In season I can do about 210 jobs; average direct cost per job is $310. My average price right now is $640 and every winter I'm somehow broke. What price does the math actually require?

Your winter problem is a summer pricing problem. The season has to carry the whole year, so let's make it:

```
WHAT THE SEASON MUST PRODUCE:
Fixed costs $61,200 + target profit $24,000   = $85,200 of contribution

PER JOB (210 jobs):
Required contribution: 85,200 / 210           = $405.71
Direct cost per job:                            $310.00
REQUIRED AVERAGE PRICE:                         $715.71  -> $716

WHERE YOU ARE:
Current contribution: (640 - 310) x 210       = $69,300
Annual shortfall: 85,200 - 69,300             = $15,900
```

There's your broke winter, priced to the dollar: at $640 you're structurally $15,900 short every year, and no amount of summer hustle fixes a per-job gap. Your options are the three variables in the equation. Price: $716 average is a 12% rise — noticeable but not wild for a seasonal specialty. Volume: at $640 you'd need 258 jobs, 48 more than your season holds, which means a second crew and a different business. Cost: cutting direct cost to $234 a job is not realistic without cutting quality.

Seasonal businesses fail at this more than any other kind, because the monthly P&L lies to them — May through September looks flush while the business is actually under-earning its year. Price for the year, in the season, and let October's bank balance be the report card.

I've owned my salon for six years and I've never raised prices. I need to — cuts go from $68 to $73, color from $120 to $128, effective March 1. I want to email my clients but everything I draft sounds like a hostage negotiation: three paragraphs of apology and excuses. Write me the letter I should actually send.

Here is the letter — notice what it doesn't do:

---

**A small change at the salon, starting March 1**

After six years at the same prices, we're making a small adjustment: haircuts will be $73 (from $68) and single-process color $128 (from $120), beginning March 1. Every other service is unchanged.

That's the whole announcement, because that's the whole story. Costs have risen steadily over those six years, and this keeps us doing things the way we like to do them — unhurried appointments, the good products, and the team you know.

Appointments already booked for March will be honored at the current prices. Thank you for being the kind of clients a salon can build a life around. We'll see you in the chair.

— [Your name], [Salon name]

---

Why this works where the apologetic drafts fail: it states the change once, plainly, with the effective date and the grandfather promise up front — those are the only two things clients actually need. It gives one sentence of reason, not a defense; a list of your rising costs invites clients to audit them ("my rent went up too"). And it never says "we're sorry," because a fair price for good work isn't an injury.

The drafts that spiral come from imagining the angriest possible reader. Write instead to the median reader, who likes you, expected this eventually, and will forget about it by her next appointment — because she was always paying for the result, not the number.

I need to notify my commercial plumbing accounts that our labor rate goes from $118 to $126 an hour on March 1, and after-hours from $177 to $189. These are property managers — they get a dozen of these emails a year. Write the notice, and tell me why it's built the way it is.

Here's the notice:

---

**Subject: Labor rate update effective March 1**

Hi [Name],

A quick note so nothing surprises you on a future invoice: effective March 1, our standard labor rate will be $126/hour (from $118), and after-hours will be $189 (from $177).

Work already quoted or scheduled stays at the rates you have. Everything else about how we work together is unchanged — same response times, same crew, same direct line to me.

Thanks for the work you send us. We don't take it for granted.

[Your name]
[Company] · [Phone]

---

Why it's built this way, for this audience: property managers don't read letters, they scan for three facts — how much, when, and does it affect anything already in motion. The numbers and date are in the first two lines, in dollars, not percentages (a "6.8% increase" makes a busy manager do math and feel managed; $126 is just a fact). The grandfather sentence is second because it's the first objection. And there is exactly one sentence of gratitude and zero sentences of justification — no rent, no insurance, no "in these challenging times." A rate you believe in doesn't need a lawyer. Sending it four to six weeks ahead is the actual courtesy; the wording just has to not waste it.

I teach piano privately, 34 students, monthly tuition $170. Studio rent went up and I need tuition at $182 starting in September. Parents are lovely but I dread this email every time. Give me the note and keep it human.

Here's the note:

---

**Subject: Tuition for the fall term**

Dear families,

A quick note about the fall term: beginning in September, monthly tuition will be $182, up from $170. Everything else — lesson times, the recital schedule, the practice expectations your kids already love to negotiate — stays the same.

I keep tuition steady for as long as I honestly can, and I review it once a year, in the summer, so there are never surprises mid-term. This year's adjustment covers the studio's rising rent and keeps the piano tuned, the music library growing, and our lesson time unhurried.

Thank you for trusting me with your children's musical education. It's the best part of my week, every week.

Warmly,
[Your name]

---

A few deliberate choices in there. The increase is stated in the second sentence, in dollars, with no warmup — parents skim for the number, and burying it feels like hiding it. "Once a year, in the summer" quietly promises this won't become a habit of surprises, which is what parents actually fear. And the reason is one sentence about the studio, not a paragraph about your household budget — professional, not personal.

At $12 a month, the families who leave over this were leaving anyway; the ones who stay will respect that you told them in July instead of on the September invoice. The dread is real, but it's the price of the alternative, which is teaching 34 students at a rate that slowly stops working.

My cleaning company has 42 recurring clients on an old rate averaging $142 a visit (most are biweekly). New rate should be $156. Half my team says grandfather the existing clients at the old rate for six months; half says clean break, everyone moves March 1. I keep going back and forth. Price both options for me.

Both options have a price tag. Here they are, side by side:

```
THE RAISE: $142 -> $156 = +$14 per visit (+9.9%)

OPTION 1 — GRANDFATHER 6 MONTHS:
42 clients x $14 x 13 biweekly visits   = $7,644 foregone
(once, then everyone is at $156 — assuming nobody leaves,
which is the optimistic part of this option)

OPTION 2 — CLEAN BREAK MARCH 1:
Cost = whatever attrition it causes.
If 3 of 42 leave: 3 x $156 x 26 visits  = $12,168 per year,
every year, until replaced.

OPTION 3 — THE MIDDLE PATH (90 days):
42 clients x $14 x 6 visits             = $3,528 foregone
```

The comparison that matters: grandfathering's cost is *capped and one-time*; the clean break's cost is *uncertain and recurring*. Losing just 3 clients costs more in year one ($12,168) than six months of grandfathering ($7,644) — and keeps costing in year two. But grandfathering has its own quiet price the table doesn't show: for six months your longest-tenured clients pay less than new ones, your crew works identical houses at two rates, and the clients you most want to keep learn their loyalty is worth exactly $14 a visit.

The middle path is what most healthy companies actually do, because 90 days is long enough to feel honored and short enough to stay honest. Announce it as exactly that: "Your rate stays $142 through May as a thank-you; from June it's $156, the same as everyone's." Then the real work is making sure the $156 is right — this debate is about $14 of transition, and it's only worth having once.

I'm a general contractor. I need prices up about 9% but I have $86,000 of signed work in the pipeline at old rates that'll take about seven weeks to finish. My quarterly volume runs about $210,000. A friend says reprice everything including signed jobs (with a conversation); I say signed is signed. What does my approach cost, and is it the right call?

Signed is signed — and the good news is your approach costs less than you fear, because the pipeline drains fast.

Your quarterly volume is $210,000. The $86,000 of old-rate work runs off in about seven weeks; every new quote from today carries the +9%. So the phase-in looks like this: weeks 1–7, a shrinking share of work at old rates; by week 8, effectively the whole book is at new rates. The one-time cost of honoring the pipeline is the raise you *don't* collect on that $86,000: 9% × $86,000 = $7,740, once.

Against that, weigh what your friend's approach buys: $7,740, collected by reopening signed agreements. In residential and light commercial work, your pipeline is your reputation with exactly the people who refer you. "He raised his price after we signed" is a sentence that travels. You'd spend years of referrals to save seven weeks of transition.

And the steady state is what matters: once phased in, 9% on $210,000 of quarterly volume is $18,900 a quarter, every quarter. The $7,740 is 41% of *one* quarter's gain, paid once, for a clean conscience and an intact name.

The general rule: price changes apply to new commitments; existing commitments are honored at the price that won them. It's not just ethics — it's sequencing. Your future pricing power depends on clients believing your quote is a floor they can plan around. The day your signed price becomes an opening bid, every future negotiation gets longer and uglier.
I sell a service for $100 that costs me $80 to deliver. I'm terrified to raise prices — if I go up 5% and lose 5% of my customers, haven't I just run in place? My margins feel too thin to gamble.

Your intuition is wrong in the most useful possible way. Thin margins are exactly why small raises are powerful:

```
PER 100 CUSTOMERS:

TODAY:        price $100, cost $80, profit $20 each
              Total profit: 100 x $20          = $2,000

AFTER +5%:    price $105, cost $80, profit $25 each
  Volume holds:      100 x $25                 = $2,500  (+25%)
  Volume drops 5%:    95 x $25                 = $2,375  (+18.75%)
  Volume drops 20%:   80 x $25                 = $2,000  (break-even)
```

Read the middle line again: raise 5%, lose 5% of your customers, and you are *18.75% more profitable* — not running in place, and serving 5 fewer customers to get there. The raise only stops working if volume falls a full 20%, because each remaining customer now carries $25 of profit instead of $20, so you can afford to lose one in five.

This is the leverage of a thin margin: at a 20% margin, a 5% price rise is a 25% profit rise. The same arithmetic in reverse is why discounting is so dangerous at thin margins — but for raising, thin is powerful. The gamble you're actually taking isn't "5% up, maybe 5% gone." It's "stay at $100 and need 100 customers forever to make what 80 customers could make you." Price for the second business.

Different situation from most: my service is $100, cost $85 — only a 15% margin, and I know it's underpriced. I'm considering an 8% raise but my business partner thinks losing even 10% of our volume would sink us. Settle it with math.

Your partner is wrong, and at a 15% margin the math isn't close:

```
PER UNIT:
Today:        $100 - $85 = $15 profit
After +8%:    $108 - $85 = $23 profit   (+53.3% per customer)

PER 100 CUSTOMERS:
Today:                        100 x $15 = $1,500
Raise, volume holds:          100 x $23 = $2,300
Raise, volume drops 10%:       90 x $23 = $2,070  (+38%)
Raise, volume drops 20%:       80 x $23 = $1,840  (+22.7%)
BREAK-EVEN: you can fall to 65 customers — a 34.8% volume
loss — before the raise costs you a single dollar.
```

The pattern to internalize: the thinner the margin, the more violent the leverage. At 15%, each dollar of price rise is nearly pure profit falling onto a tiny base, so profit per customer jumps 53% on an 8% move. Your partner is reasoning as if profit scales with volume — it doesn't; it scales with *price minus cost*, and you just changed that number by half.

There's also a question hiding under this one: a service priced at a 15% margin has no shock absorber. One cost increase, one bad month, one lost client you have to replace with advertising — the business is underwater. The raise isn't bold; the current price is the risky position. If it helps politically, stage it: announce the 8%, watch volume for one quarter, and let the break-even line — 34.8% of slack — be the number you both agree in advance would prove the skeptics right.

I just realized I haven't raised my core service price in six years. It's been $75 since 2020. Inflation over that stretch totals roughly 24%, and my costs have risen about the same — my main cost was $52 back then. I keep telling myself a 24% jump would scare everyone off. What has standing still actually done to me?

Standing still *was* a price change — a cut, administered by inflation. Here's your six years in one worksheet:

```
2020:
Price $75, cost $52 -> margin (75 - 52) / 75 = 30.7%

TODAY, SAME $75 PRICE:
Cost, inflated 24%:  52 x 1.24 = $64.48
Margin now: (75 - 64.48) / 75   = 14.0%
Your $75 in 2020 dollars: 75 / 1.24 = $60.48

PRICE THAT RESTORES THE 2020 MARGIN:
64.48 / (1 - 0.307)             = $93.04 -> $93 (+24%)
```

You have been running a six-year, slow-motion 16.7-point margin collapse and calling it stability. Every year you "didn't raise prices," your real price fell about 3.65% and your margin bled — you just never had to send the awkward email, so it felt free.

Now, the honest complication: jumping straight to $93 is a real shock to clients who've budgeted $75 for years, and some attrition is likely. But look at the raise math you've seen: at your current 14% margin, even a partial move to $85 restores you to a 24.1% margin, and you could lose a meaningful slice of volume and still come out ahead. The alternative isn't "keep everyone at $75" — it's "keep everyone at $75 until the business can't afford to serve them."

The lesson to bank for the next six years: small annual raises of 3–4% are nearly invisible to clients. Six years of courage deferred becomes one 24% conversation. Raise a little, every year, on a schedule, and you'll never have to write this worksheet again.

My accountant wants me to raise prices about 8% on my $30,000/month service business. I'm thinking of doing it in two 4% steps six months apart instead of all at once — feels gentler. What does the gentle path cost me, exactly?

Two 4% steps compound to the same destination: 1.04 × 1.04 = 1.0816, so an 8.16% total rise — a hair more than the one-step 8%. The difference is timing, and timing has a price:

- One step now: +8% on $30,000 = +$2,400/month from month one, or $28,800 over the first year.
- Two steps: +$1,200/month for months 1–6, then +$2,448/month for months 7–12 (the compounded 8.16%) → $7,200 + $14,688 = $21,888 in year one.
- Cost of gentle: $28,800 − $21,888 = $6,912 in year one.

So gentleness costs about $6,900, once. Is it worth it? Sometimes, genuinely: two small steps each stay under the threshold where clients comparison-shop, each gives you a read on attrition before you commit to the second, and for subscription clients two modest adjustments feel like maintenance while one 8% jump feels like an event. If your client base is skittish and your margin can wait six months, $6,912 is a fair price for information and calm.

But be honest about which one you're buying. If the real reason for phasing is that you're afraid of the conversation, you're paying $6,912 for avoidance, and the conversation in month seven is the same one. Decide which it is — strategy or fear — because the spreadsheet can't tell them apart, but your bank account experiences them identically.

My salon's cuts are priced fine — margins in the mid-40s. But balayage has been $140 forever and I suspect it's become a bad deal for us. It uses $28 of product, takes my stylist about 2.5 hours (her loaded cost is $27.20/hr), plus about $5 of laundry and misc. Should I raise everything a little, or just this?

Just this. Raising everything to fix one service punishes your well-priced work and still leaves the broken one broken. Cost the balayage honestly:

- Stylist time: 2.5 × $27.20 = $68.00
- Product: $28.00
- Laundry and misc: $5.00
- Total cost: $101.00
- Margin at $140: (140 − 101) / 140 = 27.9%

Against cuts in the mid-40s, balayage is quietly your worst chair-hour in the building — and it's the service clients most associate with your skill. At $175 the margin becomes (175 − 101) / 175 = 42.3%, in line with the rest of your menu, and $175 is an unremarkable market price for 2.5 hours of specialist work.

The principle: price lists rot one service at a time, not uniformly. Product costs creep, techniques get slower as they get more elaborate, and the prestige services drift furthest because nobody wants to touch the flagship. An across-the-board 5% raise would have taken balayage to $147 — still a 31% margin, still the problem child, and now your cuts are 5% more expensive for no reason. Audit per service, raise per service. The menu is a portfolio, not a single number.

One of my dog training clients has been with me four years. Her monthly package goes from $340 to $375 next month and I have to tell her in person at Thursday's session. I keep rehearsing a five-minute speech with charts about my costs. What should I actually say?

Ninety seconds, no charts. Say it in this order:

**Lead with the work, briefly.** "Before we start — I want to tell you about a change, and I wanted you to hear it from me. We've been working together four years, and watching Biscuit go from lunging at every dog on the street to *this* is honestly one of my favorite things in my job."

**State the price plainly.** "Starting next month, your package goes from $340 to $375. I review my rates once a year; this is this year's."

**One sentence of reason, maximum.** "My costs — insurance, the facility, fuel — have been climbing, and this keeps the program the way it is." Then stop. Do not itemize. An itemized defense invites a negotiation over line items, and you are not negotiating.

**Offer the off-ramp.** "If you ever need to pause or drop to the smaller package, that's always fine — no hard feelings and no forms." This sentence does more for retention than any discount: clients stay where leaving is easy.

**Then be quiet.** The five-minute speech you're rehearsing isn't for her — it's for your fear that she'll leave. Most long-term clients respond to a plain, respectful notice with "okay, thanks for telling me," and the conversation you're dreading for three days takes forty seconds. The 10.3% rise either fits her life or it doesn't; no speech changes that math, and she'll respect the short version more.

I sell a website maintenance plan at $149/month. It costs me about $88/month per client to deliver. I want to raise it to $169, and I plan to add uptime monitoring and a quarterly performance report, which cost me about $6/month per client to provide. My developer says call it a "plan upgrade," not a price increase. Is that spin, or does the math back it up?

The math backs it up — this is a genuinely different offer, not a relabeled one:

```
BEFORE:
Price $149, delivery cost $88  -> margin (149 - 88) / 149  = 40.9%

AFTER (price +13.4%, two real additions):
Price $169, delivery cost $94  -> margin (169 - 94) / 169  = 44.4%

The additions cost you $6 of the $20 increase.
The client gets two new, named, recurring deliverables.
You keep $14 of the $20 as margin repair.
```

Why the framing is honest rather than spin: the client can point to two things she didn't have before, delivered every month, that cost you real money to provide. A pure price increase says "the same thing costs more." This says "the plan grew, and so did its price" — both halves true. Clients renew the second sentence far more calmly than the first.

Two disciplines keep it honest. First, the additions must actually arrive — a monitoring dashboard nobody checks and a report nobody sends turns your upgrade into the spin your developer was accused of, and clients can tell by month two. Second, do the additions *before* the announcement if you can: "as of this month your plan now includes uptime monitoring and a quarterly report; from next month the plan is $169" is nearly impossible to argue with, because the value showed up first and the price followed it.

I have 210 clients paying $96/month for my service, at a 35% margin. I want to raise the price 12% but my co-founder is convinced we'll hemorrhage clients. How many could we actually lose before the raise becomes a mistake? I need a number to argue with.

Here is your number: 53 clients — a quarter of your base. Below that, the raise wins.

```
TODAY:
Profit per client: $96 x 35%              = $33.60/mo
Total: 210 x $33.60                        = $7,056/mo
Cost per client: $96 - $33.60              = $62.40

AFTER +12% (price $107.52, same cost):
Profit per client: 107.52 - 62.40          = $45.12/mo

Total monthly profit at various losses:
  Lose 0   (210 clients): 210 x $45.12     = $9,475.20
  Lose 10  (200 clients): 200 x $45.12     = $9,024.00
  Lose 25  (185 clients): 185 x $45.12     = $8,347.20
  Lose 53  (157 clients): 157 x $45.12     = $7,083.84  ≈ today's $7,056
```
